intro.why: Language models are the core of every modern text generator. n-gram models are the simplest working version: they introduce the probability chain, the data-sparsity problem, smoothing and perplexity, all of which carry over directly to neural and large language models.

sections.title: What a language model is and why it helps
sections.plain: A model that assigns a probability to a word sequence, or equivalently to the next word.
sections.body:
A language model (LM) computes either the probability of a whole sequence $P(W) = P(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n)$ or the probability of the next word $P(w_n\mid w_1,\dots,w_{n-1})$; the two are equivalent through the chain rule. Many systems generate several candidates and let the LM choose the most fluent:

  • Machine translation: P(high winds tonight) > P(large winds tonight).
  • Spelling correction: "about fifteen minuets from" is a real-word error; P(about fifteen minutes from) is far higher.
  • Speech recognition: P(I saw a van) ≫ P(eyes awe of an), although they sound alike.
  • Also autocomplete, summarisation, question answering, and every generative chatbot.

"Language model" originally meant exactly this n-gram probability; today's LLMs are the same idea with a neural network estimating the next-word distribution.

sections.title: The chain rule and the Markov assumption
sections.plain: Split a sentence probability into next-word probabilities, then condition only on the last few words.
sections.body:
The chain rule of probability is exact:

$$P(w_{1:n}) = \prod_{k=1}^{n} P(w_k\mid w_{1:k-1})$$

P(its water is so transparent) = P(its) · P(water | its) · P(is | its water) · P(so | its water is) · P(transparent | its water is so). We cannot estimate the last factor by counting: there are too many possible histories, and almost none of them appear in any corpus.

The Markov assumption keeps only the last n − 1 words: $P(w_k\mid w_{1:k-1}) \approx P(w_k\mid w_{k-n+1:k-1})$. A unigram model ignores history ("I want to eat healthy food" is scored word by word); a bigram model conditions on one previous word; a trigram on two. Sentences are wrapped in <s> … </s> so the first word and the end of the sentence are also predicted.

Limitation: language has long-distance dependencies. In "The computer which I had just put into the machine room on the fifth floor crashed", or "The computer(s) … is/are", agreement spans far more words than any practical n. n-grams still work surprisingly well because most constraints are local.

sections.title: Maximum-likelihood n-gram estimates
sections.plain: Count how often a word follows its history and divide by how often the history occurs.
sections.body:
$$P_{\text{MLE}}(w_n\mid w_{n-1}) = \frac{C(w_{n-1}\,w_n)}{C(w_{n-1})}$$

This relative frequency is the maximum-likelihood estimate: it makes the training corpus as probable as possible. Example corpus of three sentences:

<s> I am Sam </s>  ·  <s> Sam I am </s>  ·  <s> I do not like green eggs and ham </s>

P(I | <s>) = 2/3, P(Sam | <s>) = 1/3, P(am | I) = 2/3, P(do | I) = 1/3, P(Sam | am) = 1/2, P(</s> | Sam) = 1/2. The estimates after any history sum to 1. Trigrams generalise the same way: $P(w_n\mid w_{n-2}w_{n-1}) = C(w_{n-2}w_{n-1}w_n)/C(w_{n-2}w_{n-1})$.

sections.title: Bigrams on a restaurant corpus
sections.plain: Real bigram tables are mostly zeros; sentence probabilities are products of small numbers, so use logs.
sections.body:
A corpus of about 9,200 spoken restaurant queries ("tell me about chez panisse", "i'm looking for a good place to eat breakfast") gives unigram counts i = 2533, want = 927, to = 2417 and bigram counts such as i want = 827, want to = 608, to eat = 686, i eat = 9, i to = 0. Normalising each row by its unigram count:

bigramcountP(w | prev)
i want8270.33
want to6080.66
to eat6860.28
i eat90.0036
i to00

With P(i | <s>) = 0.25, P(english | want) = 0.0011, P(food | english) = 0.5, P(</s> | food) = 0.68:

$$P(\text{⟨s⟩ i want english food ⟨/s⟩}) = 0.25\times0.33\times0.0011\times0.5\times0.68 \approx 0.000031$$

The table encodes facts about the world (P(chinese | want) is six times P(english | want) in this corpus), grammar (want is followed by to) and the task. Log space: multiplying many probabilities underflows, so add log-probabilities instead: log P = Σ log pᵢ ≈ −10.39 here; exponentiate only if a probability is needed.

Large-scale n-gram collections (such as web-scale counts released by search companies, with n up to 5 over a trillion words) show how much data is needed before rare phrases ("serve as the incubator") get reliable counts.

sections.title: Zeros and Laplace smoothing
sections.plain: Unseen n-grams get probability 0, which ruins test sentences; add-1 gives every n-gram a small share.
sections.body:
Overfitting to the training data: n-grams seen in training ("denied the allegations", "denied the reports") get probability; perfectly good test phrases ("denied the offer", "denied the loan") get 0. One zero makes the whole test sentence probability 0 and perplexity infinite.

Add-1 (Laplace) smoothing pretends every bigram was seen once more:

$$P_{\text{Add-1}}(w_n\mid w_{n-1}) = \frac{C(w_{n-1}w_n)+1}{C(w_{n-1})+V}$$

On the restaurant corpus (V = 1446): P(want | i) = 828/3979 = 0.21 (was 0.33), P(to | i) = 1/3979 = 0.00025 (was 0), P(eat | i) = 10/3979 = 0.0025, P(to | want) = 609/2373 = 0.26, P(eat | to) = 687/3863 = 0.18.

The reconstituted count $c^* = (C + 1)\,C(w_{n-1})/(C(w_{n-1}) + V)$ shows what add-1 effectively did: C(i want) falls from 827 to about 527. Add-1 moves too much mass to the huge number of unseen pairs, so it is a blunt instrument for n-gram LMs. It is still fine where zeros are rarer, such as text classification (naive Bayes). Add-k (k < 1, tuned on held-out data) is gentler. A simple MLE example: if "bagel" appears 400 times in a million words, P_MLE(bagel) = 0.0004, best for this corpus but perhaps not for another.

sections.title: Backoff, interpolation and stupid backoff
sections.plain: Use less context when you have little evidence: either switch down to lower orders or always blend them.
sections.body:
Backoff: use the trigram if it has enough evidence; otherwise the bigram; otherwise the unigram. Interpolation: always mix all three:

$$\hat P(w_n\mid w_{n-2}w_{n-1}) = \lambda_3 P(w_n\mid w_{n-2}w_{n-1}) + \lambda_2 P(w_n\mid w_{n-1}) + \lambda_1 P(w_n),\quad \sum_i\lambda_i = 1$$

The λs may also depend on the context. They are chosen to maximise the probability of a held-out set (training data for counts, held-out data for λ, test data for final evaluation). Interpolation generally works better than plain backoff; proper backoff (Katz) must also discount higher-order probabilities so that the total still sums to 1.

Stupid backoff (for web-scale n-grams, Brants et al. 2007): if the n-gram was seen, use its relative frequency; otherwise use 0.4 × the score of the shorter n-gram, recursively down to the unigram. Scores are not probabilities (they don't sum to 1), but with enormous data this is fast and works well. Large models also prune: drop singleton n-grams or keep only those above a count threshold, and store counts efficiently.

sections.title: Unknown words and vocabulary
sections.plain: Fix a vocabulary, map everything else to <UNK>, and train <UNK> like a normal word.
sections.body:
In a closed-vocabulary task all test words are known in advance (e.g. a fixed command set). Usually the vocabulary is open: test text contains out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words never seen in training, which would otherwise get probability 0.

  1. Choose a fixed vocabulary L (e.g. all words with count ≥ 2, or the top 50,000).
  2. In training, replace every word not in L with <UNK>.
  3. Estimate <UNK>'s probabilities from those counts like any other word.
  4. At test time, map unseen words to <UNK>.

Caution: a model with a tiny vocabulary can achieve deceptively low perplexity by turning many words into a highly probable <UNK>, so perplexities are comparable only between models with the same vocabulary. Modern LMs avoid most of this with subword tokens (byte-pair encoding), so any string can be spelled from known pieces.

sections.title: Evaluation: extrinsic tests and perplexity
sections.plain: The real test is the application; the quick test is how surprised the model is by held-out text.
sections.body:
Extrinsic (in vivo) evaluation puts each model into a real task (spelling correction, speech recognition, translation) and compares task accuracy: the best test, but slow. Intrinsic evaluation measures the model directly on unseen test data. The Shannon game captures the intuition: how well can you guess the next word? "I always order pizza with cheese and ___" (mushrooms 0.1, pepperoni 0.1, … fried rice 0.0001); "The 33rd president of the US was ___"; "I saw a ___". A better model gives the actual next word higher probability.

$$PP(W) = P(w_1 w_2\dots w_N)^{-1/N} = \sqrt[N]{\prod_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{P(w_i\mid w_{i-1})}}$$

Perplexity is the inverse probability of the test set normalised by length; minimising perplexity = maximising probability. It equals the weighted average branching factor: a string of digits where each digit has probability 1/10 has perplexity exactly 10. On a newspaper corpus (38 million training words, 1.5 million test words): unigram 962, bigram 170, trigram 109.

Rules: never let test data into training (it gives falsely low perplexity), compare only with the same vocabulary, and remember lower perplexity usually, but not always, means better task performance. Common corpora for LM work include the Brown corpus, newspaper text, parliamentary proceedings, and telephone-conversation and broadcast-news transcripts.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Kneser–Ney smoothing (the classic best n-gram method) uses absolute discounting plus a "continuation" unigram: how many different contexts a word follows ("Francisco" is frequent but follows only "San").
  • Sampling from an n-gram model (the Shannon visualisation) shows its quality: unigram output is word salad; trigrams trained on a small corpus copy it.
  • Cross-entropy: log₂ PP is the average number of bits per word, linking perplexity to information theory and to the loss used to train neural LMs (M5).
  • Genre matters: an LM trained on one domain can be badly perplexed by another.

code.title: Bigram MLE and sentence probability
code.explain: Counts bigrams on the three-sentence Sam corpus, then reproduces the restaurant-query estimates, the sentence probability 0.000031 (log −10.39), and the add-1 values including the reconstituted count 827 → 527.
mistakes: Multiplying raw probabilities for long texts instead of adding logs.
code.code:
"""Maximum-likelihood bigram estimates, sentence probabilities, and add-1 smoothing.

Part 1: the tiny 'Sam' corpus. Part 2: published counts from a restaurant-query corpus (9,222 sentences).
"""
from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction
corpus = ["<s> I am Sam </s>", "<s> Sam I am </s>", "<s> I do not like green eggs and ham </s>"]
uni, bi = Counter(), Counter()
for s in corpus:
    t = s.split(); uni.update(t); bi.update(zip(t, t[1:]))
P = lambda w, prev: Fraction(bi[(prev, w)], uni[prev])
for w, prev in [("I", "<s>"), ("Sam", "<s>"), ("am", "I"), ("</s>", "Sam"), ("Sam", "am"), ("do", "I")]:
    print(f"P({w} | {prev}) = {P(w, prev)}")

# restaurant corpus: unigram counts and selected bigram counts
U = {"i": 2533, "want": 927, "to": 2417, "eat": 746, "chinese": 158, "food": 1093, "lunch": 341, "spend": 278}
B = {("i", "want"): 827, ("i", "to"): 0, ("i", "eat"): 9, ("want", "i"): 2, ("want", "to"): 608, ("to", "eat"): 686, ("i", "i"): 5}
print("\nMLE bigrams:")
for (a, b), c in B.items(): print(f"  P({b} | {a}) = {c}/{U[a]} = {c / U[a]:.4f}")
p = 0.25 * 0.33 * 0.0011 * 0.5 * 0.68
print(f"\nP(<s> i want english food </s>) = .25 x .33 x .0011 x .5 x .68 = {p:.6f}")
import math
print(f"in log space: {sum(math.log(x) for x in (0.25, 0.33, 0.0011, 0.5, 0.68)):.3f} (sum of logs, avoids underflow)")

V = 1446
print("\nAdd-1 (Laplace) with V = 1446:")
for (a, b), c in B.items():
    print(f"  P*({b} | {a}) = ({c}+1)/({U[a]}+{V}) = {(c + 1) / (U[a] + V):.5f}")
cstar = (827 + 1) * U["i"] / (U["i"] + V)
print(f"reconstituted count c*(i, want) = 828 x 2533 / 3979 = {cstar:.0f}  (real count 827)")

code.title: Smoothing and perplexity on a toy corpus
code.explain: Trains unigram, MLE bigram, add-1 and interpolated bigram models on a small generated corpus and compares their test perplexity: the MLE bigram is infinite because of one unseen pair; interpolation does best. Also checks that the digits example gives perplexity 10.
code.notes: λ is fixed here; in practice tune it on held-out data.
code.code:
"""Perplexity of unigram, bigram and interpolated models on held-out text, plus the digits example.

A small synthetic 'grammar' generates training and test sentences; we compare add-1 bigrams with
linearly interpolated bigrams (lambdas tuned on a held-out set).
"""
import math, random
from collections import Counter
random.seed(0)
subj = ["i", "we", "you"]; verb = ["want", "like", "need"]; obj = ["chinese food", "a cheap restaurant", "lunch", "to eat now", "italian food"]
def sent(): return ["<s>"] + f"{random.choice(subj)} {random.choice(verb)} {random.choice(obj)}".split() + ["</s>"]
train = [sent() for _ in range(300)]; held = [sent() for _ in range(100)]; test = [sent() for _ in range(100)]
test.append(["<s>", "we", "need", "a", "cheap", "lunch", "</s>"])            # contains an unseen bigram
uni = Counter(w for s in train for w in s); bi = Counter(p for s in train for p in zip(s, s[1:]))
V = len(uni); N = sum(uni.values())
def p_uni(w): return (uni[w] + 1) / (N + V)
def p_add1(w, prev): return (bi[(prev, w)] + 1) / (uni[prev] + V)
def p_mle(w, prev): return bi[(prev, w)] / uni[prev] if uni[prev] else 0.0
def p_interp(w, prev, l): return l * p_mle(w, prev) + (1 - l) * p_uni(w)
def pp(model, data):
    lp, n = 0.0, 0
    for s in data:
        for prev, w in zip(s, s[1:]):
            p = model(w, prev)
            if p == 0: return float("inf")
            lp += math.log2(p); n += 1
    return 2 ** (-lp / n)
best = min((pp(lambda w, pr: p_interp(w, pr, l), held), l) for l in [i / 20 for i in range(1, 20)])
print(f"vocabulary {V}, training tokens {N}")
print(f"perplexity on test: unigram {pp(lambda w, pr: p_uni(w), test):.2f} | MLE bigram {pp(p_mle, test)} | "
      f"add-1 bigram {pp(p_add1, test):.2f} | interpolated (lambda={best[1]}) {pp(lambda w, pr: p_interp(w, pr, best[1]), test):.2f}")
print("MLE gives infinite perplexity because of one unseen bigram ('cheap lunch').")
print("Digits 0-9 each with probability 1/10: perplexity =", round((0.1 ** 10) ** (-1 / 10), 6))
